source.title: The Missing Margin: How Sample Corruption Affects Distance to the Boundary in ANNs
source.authors: Marthinus W. Theunissen; Coenraad Mouton; Marelie Hattingh Davel

record.tranche_reason: Tests the width and generalization relationship in V2 with a capacity sweep and validation error, but does not report the exact original study’s full settings.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. on fitting noise and generalizing, but those cited results are not this study’s results. Its own validation and margin measurements are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The clean MNIST experiment uses the same basic method and outcome as V2: a width sweep of one-hidden-layer ReLU networks with held-out classification error measured after interpolation. Corrupted MNIST and CIFAR-10 CNN experiments extend this comparison to additional settings. Explicit regularization and convergence beyond the stated epoch budgets are not established.
record.authors_conclusion: The record largely captures the authors' conclusion: corrupted samples can have small input-space margins with different implications for generalization, so average margins require comparable sample composition. Its blanket statement that input corruption does not harm generalization needs qualification: Section 6 explicitly reports noticeably worse generalization for input-corrupted CIFAR-10 models than clean CIFAR-10 models, unlike MNIST. The proposed remoteness explanation remains speculative.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps capacity for single-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs on MNIST, including clean models, and reports held-out validation error. It also studies CNNs and corrupted datasets; the text does not state whether explicit regularization is absent.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, corruption type, sample type, and capacity change the reported margin patterns and validation performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Input-space margins generally increase with capacity, but corrupted samples have smaller margins than clean samples. Label corruption also reduces clean-sample margins; input corruption has a smaller effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Average input-space margins can obscure sample groups whose margins have different implications for generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Label corruption reduces nearest different-target distances for many samples. Gaussian input corruption usually preserves or increases these distances, especially for corrupted MNIST samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different-target proximity constrains input-space margins, while remote corrupted samples can retain small margins for other reasons.

record.peer_reviewed: SACAIR 2022 proceedings (the supplied text identifies itself as a preprint of the published paper)
record.problems: Validation results and margin curves are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. Margin analyses include only correctly classified samples. The input-corruption explanation is explicitly speculative; the paper notes the CIFAR10 distance phenomenon is less clear.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out; figure-based margin results are included as aggregate capacity-sweep rows for each dataset, model set, and sample type.

untested.parts: No fully random-label versus natural-label comparison establishing both training fit and chance-level held-out performance under random labels.

Absence of explicit regularization and training to convergence are not established. The original downsampled CIFAR-10 one-hidden-layer setting is not tested. The minimum width needed to interpolate and an interpolation-threshold peak are not located.
No matched convolutional versus fully connected comparison, locality intervention, or transferred initialization.
No optimizer comparison within a common workload and tuning budget.
No batch-size intervention or comparison of training-budget adaptations.
No magnitude-aware weight perturbations, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison against norm- and margin-based predictors.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence followed by retraining.

missing.what: Validation-error width sweeps for MNIST with 20% label corruption and with 20% Gaussian input corruption. Record each separately, including 1,000 versus 100 training epochs and the two noninterpolating label-corrupted capacities.

Validation-error capacity sweeps for clean CIFAR-10, 10% label-corrupted CIFAR-10, and 10% Gaussian-input-corrupted CIFAR-10 CNNs. Record each separately, including Adam, 500 epochs, and the two noninterpolating label-corrupted capacities.

record.verdict_notes: Only the supplied text was used. Figure graphics and numerical curves were unavailable, so directional verdicts rely on explicit prose and the Figure 1 caption. States for rows linked to no version indicate that their measures cannot establish a listed claim, not that the reported margin findings are absent.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare the same architectures and recipes trained to fit fixed random labels versus natural labels.

Only clean MNIST single-hidden-layer MLPs match the version’s setting. The paper does not state whether explicit regularization was absent, and reports validation error rather than test error. It does not test downsampled CIFAR-10 with one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks trained from scratch.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
Measures input-space distance to a decision boundary, not magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.
